# Introduction 

Do high-AI-exposure majors earn higher starting salaries? I want a career that works with AI, because I believe it's one of the biggest technological shifts of my lifetime. In this report, AI exposure measures how much a job's tasks overlap with what AI can do. It doesn't mean that the job will be replaced. As a Statistics major, I also looked at where Statistics and four related majors I've considered fall relative to other majors.

# Data and Setup

The salaries come from the U.S. Department of Education College Scorecard [-@scorecard], using bachelor's degree graduates' median earnings one year after graduation. The AI exposure comes from the AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) index by @felten2021.

A National Center for Education Statistics and Bureau of Labor Statistics crosswalk maps fields of study to the occupations their graduates tend to enter. A major's AI exposure score is the average across all occupations that it maps to. These scores are standardized, meaning that 0 is the average occupation, and each unit is one standard deviation. Only majors with both a salary and an exposure score were kept. This left 285 majors in the TidyTuesday data set (October 20, 2026), curated by Tony Galvan [-@tidytuesday2026]. 

```{r}
#| message: FALSE

library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
library(knitr)
library(broom)


base_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/"
file_path <- "2026/2026-10-20/ai_salary_majors.csv"

ai_salary_majors <- read_csv(paste0(base_url, file_path))
```

\newpage

# Exploring the data 

Across all majors, the salary ranges from about $10k to $107k. The median is about $41k and the mean is about $46k. 

The AI exposure score runs from about -1.2 to 1.4 with around half of the majors falling between 0.68 and 1.19. Most majors have an above-average exposure compared with the average occupation, with a few below. This helps explain why the scatter plot is bunched on the right. 

I've highlighted five majors. One is my own and the other four are ones that I have considered. These are all quantitative fields that I could see myself working in. 

```{r}
#| eval: FALSE 

glimpse(ai_salary_majors)
summary(ai_salary_majors)
```
```{r}
# marking specific majors of interest

majors_of_interest <- ai_salary_majors |>
  filter(field_of_study %in% c(
    "Statistics",
    "Computer Science",
    "Economics",
    "Finance and Financial Management Services",
    "Mathematics and Computer Science"
  ))

majors_of_interest |>
  mutate(median_starting_salary = scales::dollar(median_starting_salary)) |>
  select(field_of_study, median_starting_salary, ai_exposure) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Major", "Starting Salary", "AI Exposure"))
```
\newpage

# Visualizing the Data 

```{r}
#| message: FALSE
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

ai_salary_majors |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ai_exposure, y = median_starting_salary)) +
  geom_point(color = "gray70", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = lm, color = "gray30", fill = "gray85") +
  geom_point(data = majors_of_interest, aes(color = field_of_study), size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
  "Statistics" = "#CC0000",
  "Computer Science" = "#3D3D3D",
  "Mathematics and Computer Science" = "#3D3D3D",
  "Economics" = "#3D3D3D",
  "Finance and Financial Management Services" = "#3D3D3D"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Do high-AI-exposure majors earn higher starting salaries?",
    subtitle = paste("Each point is one of 285 majors.",
                 "\nHighlighted: majors I'm considering"),
    x = "AI Exposure (standardized score)",
    y = "Median Starting Salary ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")) +
  geom_label_repel(data = majors_of_interest,
                   aes(label = field_of_study,
                       color = field_of_study),
                   size = 3.5, show.legend = FALSE)
```
I was surprised to see the trend line relating median salary to AI exposure was almost completely flat. My five majors of interest are clustered on the far right either at or above the line. The fields that I've been considering are both above-average in pay and among the most AI-exposed. Because of this, I assumed that there was a strong relationship. However, across all 285 majors, that pattern doesn't hold. 

\newpage

# Is there a relationship?

```{r}
ai_salary_majors |>
  summarize(r = cor(ai_exposure, median_starting_salary)) |>
  kable(digits =3, col.names = "Correlation (r)")

salary_model <- lm(median_starting_salary ~ ai_exposure, data = ai_salary_majors)

tidy(salary_model) |>
  mutate(term = c("Intercept", "AI Exposure")) |>
  kable(digits = 3,
  col.names = c("Term", "Estimate", "Std. Error", "t", "p-value"))
```
The correlation is nearly zero (r = 0.005), and the model's slope isn't significant (p = 0.94). In this data, AI exposure explains almost none of the variation in starting salary. 

\newpage

# Does the type of AI matter?

The data set splits AI exposure into language-modeling and image-generation exposure. Overall exposure showed no relationship, but I am curious whether the two types of AI exposure behave differently.

## Reshaping the data 

```{r}
exposure_types <- ai_salary_majors |>
  select(field_of_study, median_starting_salary,
         ai_exposure_language, ai_exposure_image) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(ai_exposure_language, ai_exposure_image),
    names_to = "exposure_type",
    values_to = "exposure"
  ) |>
  mutate(exposure_type = if_else(exposure_type == "ai_exposure_language",
                                 "Language AI", "Image AI"))

stats_types <- exposure_types |>
  filter(field_of_study == "Statistics")
```

## Comparing the two types of AI Exposure

```{r}
#| message: FALSE

exposure_types |>
  group_by(exposure_type) |>
  summarize(r = cor(exposure, median_starting_salary)) |>
  kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Exposure Type", "Correlation (r)"))
```
```{r}
#| message: FALSE
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

exposure_types |>
  ggplot(aes(x = exposure, y = median_starting_salary)) +
  geom_point(color = "gray70", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, color = "gray30", fill = "gray85") +
  geom_point(data = stats_types, color = "#CC0000", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ exposure_type) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(
    title = "Salary vs. AI exposure, by type of AI",
    subtitle = "Statistics highlighted in red",
    x = "AI Exposure (standardized score)",
    y = "Median Starting Salary ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

```{r}
exposure_types |>
  group_by(exposure_type) |>
  summarize(
    predicted = predict(lm(median_starting_salary ~ exposure),
                        newdata = tibble(exposure = exposure[field_of_study == "Statistics"])),
    actual = median_starting_salary[field_of_study == "Statistics"]
  ) |>
  mutate(across(c(predicted, actual), \(x) scales::dollar(x,    accuracy = 1))) |>
  kable(digits = 0, col.names = c("Exposure Type", "Predicted Salary", "Statistics' Salary"))
```


The picture changes when exposure is split by the type of AI. Image AI exposure has a moderate positive relationship with salary (r = 0.331), and language AI exposure has a weak negative one (r = -0.155). The two types of exposure pull in opposite directions, which may help explain why the combined score was flat. For image AI exposure, the trend line predicts about $52k at Statistics' exposure level. Statistics earns about $8k more than that. For language AI exposure, the line predicts about $44k. Statistics is about $16k above the line.  

# Conclusion 

Across all 285 majors, higher AI exposure is not linked to a higher starting salary. The correlation is almost zero (r = 0.005). All five of the majors I highlighted are high-exposure and above average in pay. They range from $51,815 (Economics) to $89,651 (Math & CS). All are above the overall median of the 285 majors at about $41k. Majors with similar AI exposure such as Publishing (~$18k at 1.13) and Business Operations Support (~$17k at 0.99) pay far less, indicating other variables at play. Exposure to AI alone doesn't predict pay. The type of AI exposure appears to matter more than overall exposure. The faceted plots above suggest a positive correlation between image AI exposure and median salary, and a negative one for language AI exposure. Within high-exposure fields, the field a student chooses matters a lot. This is encouraging for me because the fields that interest me let me work with AI and pay well. 

This analysis is observational. Even where high exposure and high pay appear together, that doesn't mean that AI exposure causes higher pay. This data also explores pay one year after graduation, so it doesn't reflect long-term earnings. The sudden advancement of artificial intelligence is still rather new. As tools become more developed, this may shift.
